Reparameterisation expresses a parameter-dependent random sample as a deterministic function of the parameters and separate base noise.
This lets appropriate sampled objectives carry pathwise gradients.

## A diagonal Gaussian sample {#gaussian-sample}

For a diagonal Gaussian encoder, the network outputs a mean vector $\mu$ and positive standard deviations $\sigma$.
A latent sample can be written as

$$
  z=\mu+\sigma\odot\epsilon,
  \qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I).
$$

Here, $\odot$ means coordinatewise multiplication.
Randomness enters through $\epsilon$, while $z$ remains differentiable with respect to the encoder's outputs.
This reparameterisation lets reconstruction gradients update the encoder as well as the decoder. [VAE, §§2.3–2.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=3).

## Log variance and implementation {#implementation}

An encoder often outputs $\ell_j=\log\sigma_j^2$, an unconstrained log variance.
The standard deviation used for sampling is then $\sigma_j=\exp(\ell_j/2)$, while the variance in the KL is $\exp(\ell_j)$.
Confusing these two quantities changes both the sampled distribution and the objective.

The reconstruction expectation is estimated by [Monte Carlo sampling](expectations.qmd#latent-expectation), while the [Gaussian KL](entropy.qmd#gaussian-kl) can be calculated analytically.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Implementation: one latent sample and an analytic KL"}

The following fragment assumes tensors of shape `[batch, latent_dim]` and a decoder likelihood implemented by `reconstruction_nll`.
The reconstruction function should sum over each example's output coordinates so its scaling is consistent with the latent-coordinate KL sum.

```python
mu, log_var = encoder(example)
std = (0.5 * log_var).exp()
z = mu + std * torch.randn_like(std)
recon = reconstruction_nll(decoder(z), example)
kl = 0.5 * (mu.square() + log_var.exp()
            - 1.0 - log_var).sum(dim=-1)
loss = (recon + kl).mean()
```

A Bernoulli decoder uses binary cross-entropy for its negative log-likelihood, whereas a Gaussian decoder with fixed variance produces scaled squared error.
A sigmoid output followed by binary cross-entropy therefore specifies a different likelihood from a Gaussian reconstruction model. [VAE, §3 and Appendix C](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.6114#page=5).

:::

## Pathwise gradient {#pathwise-gradient}

Let $z=g_\phi(\epsilon)$ have distribution $q_\phi$, with base noise independent of $\phi$ and a differentiable integrand $h$.
Under conditions allowing differentiation under the expectation, reparameterisation gives the pathwise identity

$$
  \nabla_\phi\mathbb E_{q_\phi}[h(z)]
  =\mathbb E_{\epsilon}
  [\nabla_\phi h(g_\phi(\epsilon))].
$$

The base noise distribution does not depend on $\phi$, so automatic differentiation follows the deterministic map $g_\phi$ for each sampled noise vector.
Other gradient estimators exist; the VAE contribution is a useful differentiable estimator for suitable continuous latent variables.
